newsitem.title: FRANCE: France calls for "security framework" in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: France calls for "security framework" in Zaire.

text.p: France called on the international community on Thursday to consider setting up a "security framework" for Zaire -- code words for a multinational intervention force -- and said it was ready to contribute.

"If there is no ceasefire, the international community must consider setting up a security framework (to help delivery of) humanitarian aid," foreign ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told a news briefing.
"France is ready to assume its responsibilities and we are asking our partners how available they are to join," he said.
Paris said on Wednesday it was asking its European partners to get involved in creating an airlift of humanitarian supplies to Kisangani and eastern Zaire.
The "security framework" would protect delivery of the supplies in areas threatened by the advance of Tutsi-led rebels against government forces.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, who is advancing on Kisangani in a challenge to Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, has accepted a U.N. peace plan as a basis for talks but rejected its call for a ceasefire.
A senior French defence ministry official told reporters that an international airlift was still feasible since Kisangani itself was not in an immediate combat zone.

But he pointedly added that the French military had no plans to set up an airlift unilaterally. France's own airlift capacity is insufficient to make a major difference in bringing supplies to the area.

Reports that U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was unhappy with options offered her regarding Zaire and had directed U.S. experts to rethink plans to help resolve the crisis were welcomed by Rummelhardt.
"The United States share with us the belief that the current situation is unacceptable and fighting must halt as soon as possible," he said.
Officials in Washington told Reuters Albright's thoughts did not necessarily mean the United States would reverse its opposition to a multi-national force to intervene in Zaire.
French President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday denounced a "conspiracy of silence" on Zaire and appealed to the foreign states to force a ceasefire and take emergency humanitarian action.
Rummelhardt said the United States had assured Paris that it was now using its influence to stop the fighting.
Critics of French policy say Paris' main motivation is to block the rebel advance and save Mobutu, long allied to Paris.
European Union Commissioner for Humanitarian Action Emma Bonino meanwhile said she did not believe the multinational force would get off the ground.
"I don't believe anyone has the intention of putting soliders on the ground in a situation that has become so complicated," she told Radio Luxembourg.
Bonino was scathing about the failure of European Union nations to present a joint foreign or defence policy. "They prefer 15 separate national foreign policies.
"The confusion is obvious and the inefficiency was demonstrated before in ex-Yugoslavia, now in Africa and, I fear, even in Albania," she said.
